lesson.title: Fixing Carbon at Night: The CAM Strategy
lesson.summary: CAM plants separate carbon dioxide capture from the Calvin cycle by time rather than by cell type, opening their stomata only at night to minimize water loss while still feeding concentrated carbon dioxide to RuBisCO during the day.
lesson.body:
C4 plants, covered in the previous chapter, solve the photorespiration problem by separating initial carbon fixation and the Calvin cycle into two different cell types operating at the same time. Plants using Crassulacean Acid Metabolism, or CAM, named for the stonecrop family Crassulaceae where the pathway was first identified, solve essentially the same problem with the opposite strategy: they keep both steps in the same cell type but separate them in time instead, running them at different points in the day-night cycle.

A CAM plant opens its stomata at night, when cooler temperatures and higher humidity mean far less water is lost to the air for every molecule of carbon dioxide taken in. Just as in C4 plants, this nighttime carbon dioxide is fixed by PEP carboxylase, attaching it to phosphoenolpyruvate to form the four-carbon compound oxaloacetate, which gets converted to malate. Rather than shuttling this molecule to a neighboring cell, though, the CAM plant simply pumps it into its own large central vacuole and stores it there overnight as malic acid, which is why the tissues of many CAM plants taste noticeably more acidic in the early morning than later in the day.

During the day, the plant does the opposite: stomata close tightly to conserve water in the heat and dryness, sealing the leaf off from atmospheric carbon dioxide almost entirely. With the light reactions now running and generating ATP and NADPH, the plant draws the stored malate back out of the vacuole and breaks it down, releasing a burst of concentrated carbon dioxide directly inside the same cell where RuBisCO and the Calvin cycle are working. That local spike in carbon dioxide concentration pushes RuBisCO toward its carboxylase activity and away from its oxygenase activity, suppressing photorespiration in essentially the same chemical way the C4 strategy does, just achieved through a storage tank and a clock rather than a second cell type.

This time-shifted strategy is especially suited to plants adapted to extremely arid environments, since it allows nearly all gas exchange to happen during the coolest, most humid part of the day, minimizing water loss far more aggressively than either the C3 or C4 strategy can manage. Cacti, agaves, and other succulents are classic CAM plants, and their thick, water-storing tissues work alongside this nighttime carbon capture strategy as part of a broader set of adaptations to survive with very little available water.

The tradeoff is speed. Because carbon dioxide can only be captured during part of the day and has to be stored and released rather than used immediately, CAM plants generally grow more slowly than C3 or C4 plants under favorable conditions, which is a reasonable price to pay in habitats where the alternative is not slow growth but no survival at all. Comparing CAM and C4 side by side makes a broader point: two very different evolutionary solutions, one organized around space and one around time, can independently arrive at the same underlying fix for the same problem that RuBisCO's oxygenase activity creates.
